::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 4 · Lesson 6 · About 90 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Minimum path"}
Read "The problem", "Theory" and "In the project". The trade-offs section *(deep dive)* is worth coming back to before you start a project of your own.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: departments in a shop"}
A small shop has one counter. A department store has departments (shoes, kitchen, books), each with its own staff, all under one roof and one entrance. Customers find things faster, and staff know exactly what's theirs.

But a store can also overdo it: if buying socks means queuing at a "footwear enquiries" desk, which sends you to a "hosiery fulfilment" desk, which hands you to the till, the departments have become obstacles.

A **router** is a department of your API: all the routes for one resource, in one file, with a shared address prefix. The app is the building that puts the departments together. This lesson is about having the right number of departments.
:::

## The problem

With every route written inside `create_app`, `app.py` grows by a screenful with each feature. By the end of this part it would hold about 25 routes, and every change would touch the same file. Splitting it is the obvious fix, and splitting it carelessly creates two new problems.

**Problem 1: circular imports.** Suppose `routes/users.py` needs a helper that lives in `app.py`, say the function that formats error bodies:

```python
# routes/users.py
from atlas.api.app import error_body
```

But `app.py` imports `routes/users.py` to include its router. Python now has a loop. What happens depends on which module is imported first:

```text
$ uv run python -c "import atlas.api.routes.users"

$ uv run python -c "import atlas.api.app"
ImportError: cannot import name 'error_body' from partially initialized module 'atlas.api.app' (most likely due to a circular import) (.../src/atlas/api/app.py)
```

Importing `users.py` first works, by luck. Importing `app.py` first fails, and that's exactly what Uvicorn does at startup. Python ran `app.py` from the top, reached the import of `routes/users.py`, started running it, and `users.py` asked `app.py` for `error_body`, which hadn't been defined yet: the module was "partially initialized". The test suite fails the same way before running a single test, because `conftest.py` imports `create_app`:

```text
$ uv run pytest -q
...
E   ImportError: cannot import name 'error_body' from partially initialized module 'atlas.api.app' (most likely due to a circular import) ...
```

**Problem 2: layers that do nothing.** Many project templates split every feature into a route, a "service" and a "repository". It looks organised. Here is Atlas's "get an issue or answer 404", written both ways and run against the same database:

```text
get_issue_or_404  issue 1 -> #20 'Support new metric', issue 999 -> 404
get_issue_route   issue 1 -> #20 'Support new metric', issue 999 -> 404
```

Same behaviour. The direct version is 8 lines of code; the layered one is 24, in three classes, plus an exception that exists only to be translated into another exception. ("Trade-offs" below shows both.) Every reader now has to open three places to learn one thing.

So the job is to split along the right lines: few enough pieces to hold in your head, with imports that point one way.

## Theory

### Routers

FastAPI's **`APIRouter`** is a group of routes defined in its own module and attached to the app with `app.include_router(...)`. A router sets a `prefix` (`/issues`) and `tags` (for the docs page) once for all its routes. Everything else works the same as `@app.get`: parameters, dependencies, response models.

### Resource-shaped URLs

**REST** (Representational State Transfer, more in lesson 4.18) is the dominant style for HTTP APIs. Its core habit: URLs name **resources** (nouns), and HTTP methods say what to do with them (verbs).

| Method and path | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `GET /issues` | list issues |
| `GET /issues/42` | one issue |
| `PUT /issues/42/saved` | mark issue 42 as saved (for me) |
| `DELETE /issues/42/saved` | unsave it |
| `POST /repos` | add a repository |
| `GET /users/me` | the signed-in user |

Not `/getIssues` or `/saveIssue?id=42`: the method already says "get" or "save". One router per resource family (`/auth`, `/users`, `/repos`, `/issues`, `/search`) gives one file per family.

### Imports point one way

Circular imports disappear when imports only ever point "down" a fixed order:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  APP["app.py<br/>create_app assembles everything<br/>(nothing imports it)"] --> ROUTES["routes/*.py<br/>one router per resource"]
  ROUTES --> DEPS["deps.py<br/>settings, session, current user"]
  ROUTES --> SCHEMAS["schemas.py<br/>request and response shapes"]
  DEPS --> CORE["config.py, models.py, security.py, storage.py<br/>no FastAPI, no HTTP"]
  ROUTES --> CORE
```

- `app.py` imports routers; **nothing imports `app.py`**.
- Route modules import shared pieces (`deps.py`, `schemas.py`) and the core. They rarely import each other, and only for small helpers like `issue_out`, which one resource reuses from another.
- The core modules don't know HTTP exists, so the command line and the background worker (Part 5) use them too.

The fix for Problem 1, then, is to move `error_body` to a module lower in the order, or keep error formatting entirely inside `app.py`, which is what Atlas does in lesson 4.14.

### Deep modules, not many layers

A useful test for any function, class or file: compare what you must *know to use it* (its **interface**) with what it *does for you*. A **deep** module has a small interface and does a lot: `storage.chunk_search_statement(repo, query, kind=..., limit=..., offset=...)` hides a full-text query with ranking, filtering and paging. A **shallow** module has an interface about as big as its body: `IssueRepository.get(issue_id)` is a renamed `session.get`. Shallow modules add places to look without removing anything to understand.

## In the project

### Atlas's layout

```text
src/atlas/
  config.py          settings (lesson 4.2)
  models.py          tables (Part 3, plus users in 4.7)
  storage.py         database queries shared by CLI and API (Part 3)
  security.py        hashing and tokens, no FastAPI imports (4.7, 4.8)
  github_oauth.py    GitHub sign-in (4.9)
  api/
    app.py           create_app: middleware, error handlers, routers
    deps.py          dependencies: settings, session, current user
    schemas.py       request and response shapes
    idempotency.py   safe retries (4.16)
    routes/
      auth.py        /auth/...
      users.py       /users/me...
      repos.py       /repos
      issues.py      /issues...
      search.py      /search
      notes.py       notes (4.20)
```

The rule behind it: **code that knows about HTTP lives in `api/`; code that doesn't, lives outside.** Most of these files are filled in by later lessons; this lesson creates the shape.

### A router module

`src/atlas/api/routes/search.py` (lesson 4.12 fills in the query):

```python
"""Keyword search over an indexed codebase (the same query as `atlas find`)."""

from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter(prefix="/search", tags=["search"])


@router.get("", response_model=SearchPage)
def search(session: SessionDep, q: str, ...) -> SearchPage:
    ...
```

`@router.get("")` with `prefix="/search"` answers `GET /search`. Every module in `routes/` exposes a variable named `router`, so `create_app` attaches them in one loop:

```python
from atlas.api.routes import auth, issues, notes, repos, search, users

for module in (auth, users, repos, issues, notes, search):
    app.include_router(module.router)
```

`/health` and `/ready` stay in `app.py`: they're about the process, not a resource, and there are only two.

### Refactoring under tests

Moving code between files changes no behaviour, so it's the **refactor** step of lesson 4.5's loop: no new test, but the existing suite must pass before and after. After the move:

```text
$ uv run pytest tests/test_api_operations.py tests/test_schemas.py -q
18 passed in 1.39s
```

If an import were wrong or a router weren't included, these tests would say so at once. That's why lesson 4.5 came before this one.

Once all of Part 4 is in place, the OpenAPI document lists these paths:

```text
$ curl -s http://localhost:8000/openapi.json | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(sorted(json.load(sys.stdin)[\"paths\"]))"
['/auth/login', '/auth/logout', '/auth/refresh', '/auth/register', '/health', '/issues', '/issues/{issue_id}', '/issues/{issue_id}/notes', '/issues/{issue_id}/saved', '/notes/{note_id}', '/ready', '/repos', '/search', '/users/me', '/users/me/saved-issues']
```

(The GitHub sign-in routes are hidden from the docs with `include_in_schema=False`: they're browser redirects, not calls a client makes.)

## Trade-offs: layers versus deep modules *(deep dive)*

Here is the counter-example from "The problem" in full. The layered version:

```python
class IssueRepository:
    def __init__(self, session: Session) -> None:
        self.session = session

    def get(self, issue_id: int) -> Issue | None:
        return self.session.get(Issue, issue_id, options=[selectinload(Issue.labels)])


class IssueNotFound(Exception):
    pass


class IssueService:
    def __init__(self, repository: IssueRepository) -> None:
        self.repository = repository

    def get_issue(self, issue_id: int) -> Issue:
        issue = self.repository.get(issue_id)
        if issue is None:
            raise IssueNotFound(issue_id)
        return issue


def get_issue_route(session: Session, issue_id: int) -> Issue:
    service = IssueService(IssueRepository(session))
    try:
        return service.get_issue(issue_id)
    except IssueNotFound:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND, f"Issue {issue_id} not found") from None
```

And Atlas's:

```python
def get_issue_or_404(session: Session, issue_id: int) -> Issue:
    issue = session.get(Issue, issue_id, options=[selectinload(Issue.labels)])
    if issue is None:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND, f"Issue {issue_id} not found")
    return issue
```

The usual arguments for layers, and how they apply to Atlas:

| Argument for layers | Holds when | In Atlas |
|---|---|---|
| "We can swap the database" | you really have two storage back ends | One Postgres, by decision D8; SQLAlchemy already hides the driver |
| "Business logic stays out of HTTP code" | the logic is substantial and reused | Substantial logic (search, issue storage) already lives in `storage.py`, used by CLI and API |
| "Easier to test" | the layer can be tested alone, meaningfully | Tests run real routes against a real Postgres in milliseconds (lesson 4.5); a mocked repository would test the mocks |
| "Every feature looks the same" | many people, very different features | Conventions (`deps.py`, schemas, one router per resource) give the same consistency |

So Atlas adds a layer only when it would be **deep**: when it hides real complexity behind a small interface, the way `storage.py` hides full-text search or `security.py` hides token signing. If one day a rule like "an issue may be saved only if its repository is still tracked and the user hasn't hit their limit" appears in three routes, it earns a function of its own then, not before.

## Common mistakes

- **Importing `app.py` from anywhere else.** It sits at the top of the order: it imports, it's never imported.
- **Verbs in URLs**: `/issues/42/save` with POST. Use the resource (`/issues/42/saved`) and let the method be the verb.
- **Thin pass-through layers**: three files, one line of logic.
- **Forgetting `include_router`**: the routes exist in the module but answer 404.
- **Inconsistent plurals**: `/issue/42` and `/repos`. Pick plural nouns everywhere.
- **Refactoring without running the tests**: a move that "obviously changes nothing" is when an import goes missing.

## Check yourself

**1.** Why did `import atlas.api.routes.users` succeed but `import atlas.api.app` fail?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Python runs a module top to bottom on its first import. Starting from `users.py`, Python ran all of `app.py` (whose import of `users.py` got the half-run module already in progress), so `error_body` existed by the time `users.py` asked for it. Starting from `app.py`, Python reached the router import before defining `error_body`, so `users.py` asked a half-run `app.py` for a name that didn't exist yet. Circular imports succeed or fail depending on order, which is why they must be designed out, not tested around.
:::

**2.** What makes a module "deep"? Give one deep and one shallow example from this lesson.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A deep module does a lot behind a small interface. Deep: `storage.chunk_search_statement`, which hides ranked full-text search, filtering and paging behind a few arguments. Shallow: `IssueRepository.get`, whose interface (an issue id in, an issue or `None` out) is the same as the one line it wraps.
:::

**3.** Design the URL and method for "list the notes I wrote on issue 42".

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`GET /issues/42/notes`: notes are a sub-resource of the issue, and GET reads. This is exactly what Atlas builds in lesson 4.20.
:::

## Exercise

Move the `/stats` route from lesson 4.4's exercise into `routes/stats.py` with its own router (`prefix="/stats"`, `tags=["operations"]`) and include it in `create_app`. First write a test that `GET /stats` answers 200 with both keys, and run it before the route exists to see it fail with 404.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from fastapi import APIRouter
from sqlalchemy import func, select

from atlas.api.deps import SessionDep
from atlas.models import Chunk, Repo

router = APIRouter(prefix="/stats", tags=["operations"])


@router.get("")
def stats(session: SessionDep) -> dict[str, int]:
    repos = session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Repo)) or 0
    chunks = session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Chunk)) or 0
    return {"repos": repos, "chunks": chunks}
```
Add `stats` to the import and the `for module in (...)` loop. The test: `response = client.get("/stats")`, then `assert response.status_code == 200` and `assert set(response.json()) == {"repos", "chunks"}`. With an empty test database both counts are 0. Not in the reference code.
:::

## Stretch

Sketch REST URLs for Part 6's features: asking a question about a repository, listing past answers, and rating an answer as helpful. Which method does each use, and which router would own each?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
One reasonable design: `POST /repos/{repo_id}/questions` (ask; creates a question and its answer), `GET /questions` (my past questions), `GET /questions/{id}` (one with its answer), `PUT /questions/{id}/rating` with `{"helpful": true}` (set my rating; idempotent). A `questions` router would own all four, even the first: the resource being created is a question, and the repository is only part of its address. Part 6 builds its own version and explains its choices.
:::

## What changed in the project

New `src/atlas/api/routes/` package with one router per resource; `create_app` includes them. Commit: `refactor: Split the API into routers`.
